procedural_history.originating_court: City Magistrate and Additional District Magistrate, Lashkar
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated September 11, 1953, of the former Madhya Bharat High Court in Appeals Nos. 42 and 43 of 1953.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent preferred two appeals to the High Court of Madhya Bharat against his convictions under s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court consolidated the appeals and, applying the doctrine of autrefois acquit, held that since the trial court had found the respondent not guilty of an offence under s. 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act based on the same facts, it was tantamount to an acquittal for that offence, precluding a conviction under s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court acquitted the respondent.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State was granted special leave to appeal against the orders of acquittal by the High Court.

decision.conviction_status: The order of the High Court acquitting the respondent of an offence under s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code is set aside.
directions: The appeals are remanded to the High Court of Madhya Pradesh for re-hearing on the merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether the offence under s. 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and the offence under s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code are the same.

facts: An accused person was tried by a Special Judge for offences under both s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and s. 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
The Special Judge convicted the accused under s. 409 IPC but acquitted him of the charge under s. 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, citing a procedural defect in the investigation.

On appeal, the High Court overturned the conviction under s. 409 IPC, reasoning that since the accused was acquitted under s. 5(2), the doctrine of 'autrefois acquit' (double jeopardy) prevented a conviction under s. 409 on the same facts, as it considered the two offences to be the same.
law: Section 409 of the Indian Penal Code defines the offence of criminal breach of trust by a public servant.
Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, defines the offence of criminal misconduct.

The doctrine of 'autrefois acquit' (double jeopardy), codified in s. 403 of the Criminal Procedure Code and Article 20 of the Constitution, prohibits a person from being tried and punished for the same offence more than once.
application: The Supreme Court held that the two offences are distinct and separate.

It reasoned that the offence of 'criminal misconduct' under s. 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act is a new offence created by that specific law and is not identical in "essence, import and content" with the offence of criminal breach of trust under s. 409 of the IPC.
The Court clarified that the Prevention of Corruption Act does not repeal or abrogate s. 409 of the IPC.

Because the offences are not the same, the principle of double jeopardy ('autrefois acquit') does not apply. An acquittal for one offence does not legally bar a conviction for the other, even if they arise from the same trial and facts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the offence under s. 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and the offence under s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code are not the same. They are distinct and separate offences. Therefore, the High Court was wrong to hold that an acquittal under s. 5(2) would bar a conviction under s. 409.

issue.issue_text: Whether an acquittal of a charge under s. 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act would bar the conviction of the accused under s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code in the same trial, based on the principles of autrefois acquit (s. 403 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) or double jeopardy (Article 20 of the Constitution).

facts: An accused was tried by a Special Judge in a single trial for two offences: criminal breach of trust under s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and criminal misconduct under s. 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act (PCA).
The trial judge convicted the accused under s. 409 IPC but held that he could not be tried for the offence under s. 5(2) PCA due to a procedural defect in the investigation.
On appeal, the High Court treated the trial judge's finding on the s. 5(2) charge as an acquittal.

Applying the doctrine of 'autrefois acquit' (a person cannot be tried again for the same offence after being acquitted), the High Court set aside the conviction under s. 409 IPC, reasoning that since the accused was acquitted of the PCA charge on the same facts, he could not be convicted of the IPC charge.

law.name: s. 403 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Autrefois acquit)
law.description: Prohibits a person who has been tried and acquitted or convicted of an offence from being tried again for the same offence in a subsequent trial.

law.name: Article 20(2) of the Constitution of India (Double Jeopardy)
law.description: States that no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.

law.name: s. 26 of the General Clauses Act
law.description: Provides that where an act constitutes an offence under two or more laws, the offender can be prosecuted under either law but shall not be punished twice for the same offence.

application: The Supreme Court first established that the offences under s. 409 IPC and s. 5(2) PCA are distinct and separate. Therefore, an acquittal for one does not automatically bar a conviction for the other.

The Court held that the principle of 'autrefois acquit' under s. 403 CrPC was not applicable. This principle is designed to prevent a *subsequent trial* for the same offence. In this case, there was only a *single trial* for several offences, where the accused was acquitted of one charge and convicted of another. The rule does not apply within the same trial.

Similarly, the Court found that Article 20(2) on double jeopardy did not apply. This constitutional protection is against being prosecuted and punished for the same offence in a second trial after having already been tried and acquitted in an earlier one. Since this was a single proceeding, there was no second prosecution.

The Court affirmed the principle that when an accused faces two alternative charges in the same trial, an acquittal on one charge does not prevent a conviction on the other. It cited s. 26 of the General Clauses Act to support that there is no issue of double jeopardy in such a scenario.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's reasoning. It held that the acquittal of the charge under s. 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act did not bar the conviction of the accused under s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code in the same trial, as the principles of autrefois acquit and double jeopardy apply to subsequent trials, not to different outcomes for distinct charges within a single trial. The High Court's order of acquittal was set aside.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the offence under s. 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and the offence under s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code are the same.
appellant_arguments: The offence under s. 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and the offence under s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code are not the same.
The offence of criminal misconduct under the Prevention of Corruption Act is a new offence and does not repeal or abrogate s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code.
respondent_arguments: The two offences are the same, and therefore an acquittal under one bars a conviction under the other based on the same facts.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an acquittal of a charge under s. 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act would bar the conviction of the accused under s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code in the same trial, based on the principles of autrefois acquit (s. 403 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) or double jeopardy (Article 20 of the Constitution).
appellant_arguments: When there are two alternative charges in the same trial, an acquittal on one charge is not an impediment to a conviction on the other.
The principles of autrefois acquit (s. 403 CrPC) and double jeopardy (Article 20) do not apply because there was only one trial, not a subsequent prosecution after a previous acquittal.
respondent_arguments: The acquittal for the offence under s. 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, even in the same trial, bars a conviction under s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code based on the doctrine of autrefois acquit.

cases.case_name: Om Prakash Gupta v. The State of U.P.
cases.principle: The offence under s. 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act is distinct and separate from the one under s. 405 of the Indian Penal Code, and therefore the former does not repeal the latter.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The offence of criminal misconduct under the Prevention of Corruption Act is a distinct and separate offence from criminal breach of trust under Section 409 of the Indian Penal Code. Therefore, the principle of double jeopardy does not apply, and an acquittal for an offence under one act does not bar a conviction under the other, even if both charges arise from the same facts.
obiter: The Special Judge had jurisdiction to try the accused person under s. 7 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The view taken by the High Court that the two offences are one and the same is wrong. Consequently, there can be no objection to a trial and conviction under s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code, even if the respondent has been acquitted of an offence under s. 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The offence of criminal misconduct under the Prevention of Corruption Act is a new and distinct offence that does not repeal or abrogate s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code.
legal_tests_applied: The precedent set in Om Prakash Gupta v. The State of U. P., which held that the offence under s. 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act is distinct and separate from the one under s. 405 of the Indian Penal Code.

The test for autrefois acquit under s. 403(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code, which only prohibits a subsequent trial for the same offence and has no application where there is only one trial for several offences, with acquittal on some and conviction on another.

The test for double jeopardy under Article 20 of the Constitution, which does not apply because the respondent was not prosecuted after having already been tried and acquitted for the same offence in an earlier trial.

Section 26 of the General Clauses Act, which provides that where an act is an offence under two or more enactments, the offender may be prosecuted under any of them but shall not be punished twice for the same offence. This supports the principle that an acquittal on one of two alternate charges in the same trial does not prevent a conviction on the other.
policy_considerations: The court referenced the maxim "Nemo debet bis vexari, si constat curice quod sit pro una et eadem causa" (No man shall be twice punished, if it appears to the court that it is for one and the same cause), which is embodied in Article 20, but found it inapplicable to the facts of a single trial with alternative charges.

The application of Section 26 of the General Clauses Act reflects the policy of allowing prosecution for an act under multiple applicable laws while upholding the principle against double punishment for the same offence.
